President Trump on Thursday downplayed the importance of Russia and China's intelligence sharing with Iran amid reports that Tehran's allies have helped it target U.S. military bases.

Mr. Trump, during a short press conference with reporters at his Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida, noted that the Iran conflict had been discussed during his recent trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"My meeting with President Xi was an incredible meeting. I think that they're very little involved with Iran. They could get involved, but involvement to me would mean shooting, not giving them little information," Mr. Trump said.

He added: "We do the same thing, by the way. And you know, when they say that they may be spying on us, well, we spy on them too."

Regarding Russia's intelligence sharing, Mr. Trump said, "I don't think they give very much."

He said both countries want to see the conflict with Iran end.

"I think they're helping me in that regard," Mr. Trump said.

Days after the Iran war broke out, multiple sources, including a senior U.S. official, told CBS News that Russia was providing intelligence to Iran regarding U.S. positions in the Middle East.

national.title: Can luxury save Macy's?
national.summary: This week's celebration of Macy's 100th Thanksgiving parade finds the department store at a turning point. After years of losing sales, the retailer is reimagining itself — as a higher-end destination.
national.body:
Leaving the Macy's flagship store in New York, the Niesig family visiting from Germany sizes up their loot: a pair of sweatpants for mom, a Hurley jacket for dad, Ugg boots for their daughter. Son Mika, 16, is the only one empty-handed.

"I like zipper hoodies, and there was one zipper from Levi's that was pretty cool," he says. "But in the end, I didn't buy it because it was just a little boring."

Only on NPR What to know before using AI agents for Black Friday shopping As Macy's this week celebrates the 100th edition of its Thanksgiving Day Parade , the department store finds itself at a turning point. After years of questionable financial prospects, Macy's is trying to reinvent — as a luxury destination.

The retailer's gambit is to keep its old shoppers while also attracting new customers, who will perhaps pay more for real leather and upscale brands.

Long before the pandemic, Macy's was grappling with America's shrinking middle class — and its own lack of fresh vision.

The department store business, to begin with, has become challenging. Big store space is expensive. Online competition is stiff. Shoppers are increasingly buying directly from their favorite brands.

And Macy's faces its own struggle. The chain is neither a discounter like Kohl's or T.J.Maxx, nor an upscale store like Bergdorf Goodman or Nordstrom. Macy's has languished in between.

Pop Culture Here's how the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is brought to life "They were kind of like right in the middle," says Michael Prendergast, who advises retailers and brands at the consulting firm Alvarez & Marsal. "Now over time, that middle tier basically got crushed."

national.title: Screen free tweens try their hand at Dungeons & Dragons
national.summary: Some parents, fed up with screens, have found an analog oasis in the role-playing game invented in the 1970s.
national.body:
First published in 1974, Dungeons & Dragons is now being embraced by a new generation looking for a screen-free hobby. Lauren Migaki/NPR hide caption

Dungeons & Dragons has captivated players for more than fifty years.

In its early days, some parents complained that the role-playing game kept kids holed up inside for hours at a time. NPR even did a 10 minute piece on it in 1979. In recent years, D&D has come back into popular culture through shows like Stranger Things , a 2023 blockbuster movie and an influx of interest during the COVID-19 lockdowns .

Now, what was once a nerdy pastime has become a screen-free parent's dream – a game that relies on imagination, a role of the dice and in-person communication.

Culture Dungeons & Dragons turns 50 this year. Here's what the game has meant to you "It's a great concoction," Ted Fair says. He's the (grown-up) Dungeon Master for a group of nine to 12-year-old kids in Washington Heights in New York. "When you're able to sit down with … other people and harmonize like that."

Fair's group is part of Tweens Without Screens , a parent collective that focuses on providing technology-free activities for kids. They host things like knitting clubs and urban hikes. They have multiple D&D groups that meet monthly.

Rose Watson (left) with her brother, Leo Watson, Amos Slodounik and Benjamin Cho, are members of a D&D group hosted by Tweens Without Screens Sequoia Carrillo/NPR hide caption

"I feel like part of what's kind of fun about it is we're trying to figure it out as we go along," said Rose Watson, a 12-year-old member of Fair's D&D crew.

national.title: Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
national.summary: Ukraine's president voices frustration with US and says it is not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks to end the war.
national.body:
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.

In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin.

"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.

"He's an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.

Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.

Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.

The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.

On Thursday, Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".

national.title: Guinea-Bissau's military leaders delay return to civilian rule until 2028
national.summary: The announcement comes a year after a military coup with its leaders promising a return to civilian rule within 12 months.
national.body:
Guinea-Bissau's military rulers have postponed elections scheduled for next week by two years, delaying the return to civilian rule.

Transitional President Gen Horta N'Tam announced in a decree that the presidential and parliamentary elections, originally due on 6 December, would now take place on 26 November 2028.

The announcement came exactly a year after the military seized power, promising to return the country to civilian rule within 12 months.

In a statement, the presidency said an assessment of electoral preparations had found that there were insufficient "technical, material and financial conditions" to hold the polls as planned.

It said the delay would provide more time to ensure the elections were credible, transparent and inclusive, with all candidates given equal opportunities.

The presidency also reiterated its commitment to holding the country's first-ever local government elections but gave no date for the vote.

Gen N'Tam was sworn in as transitional president a day after the military overthrew President Umaro Sissoco Embaló in November 2025.

The coup took place three days after general elections and a day before provisional results were due to be announced.

national.title: Eagles rally to stun Cowboys coming back from 21 points behind
national.summary: Eagles QB Joe Milton threw two long touchdowns against the quarterback's former team, the Dallas Cowboys, for the the start of quite a comeback, after being down 31-10 early in the third quarter.
national.body:
Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Joe Milton III (14) runs against the Dallas Cowboys in the second half during an NFL football game in Arlington, Texas, Thursday, Nov. 26, 2026. Julio Cortez/AP hide caption

ARLINGTON, Texas — Joe Milton rolled to his left while motioning DeVonta Smith where to go near the end zone, then threw the kind of deep ball the Dallas Cowboys always knew he was capable of when he was playing for them.

That 50-yarder was the first of two long touchdowns for the Philadelphia duo against the quarterback's former team, and the start of quite a comeback.

Milton, who was Dak Prescott's backup all last season, threw three touchdowns and ran for another one in a 39-38 win Thursday in his third start for the Eagles, who signed him off the Dallas practice squad on Oct. 16.

"The guy's a rock star. ... True example of being cool, calm, collected, and just keep playing the next play, no matter what the outcome," said Eagles tackle Jordan Mailata, who was then asked about the long TD passes. "We've seen it in practice a couple of times. The oohs and aahs were still there, but not as much. It was just like you know he can get that throw done."

After 50- and 45-yard touchdown passes to Smith, Milton ran 15 yards for a score in the fourth quarter and threw a 24-yard TD to Makai Lemon with 2:10 left before Philadelphia lined up for a 2-point conversion. Milton connected with Smith in the end zone, but a holding call against Mailata wiped out the tying score before another try was broken up at the goal line.

But the Eagles (4-7), who were down 31-10 early in the third quarter, got one more chance after sacking Prescott on fourth-and-1 for a nine-yard loss to their 48 in the final minute. After a couple of short completions to Smith and a pass interference call against Dallas, Jake Elliott kicked a 59-yard field goal with 2 seconds left.

Milton, signed by the Eagles about the same time they were determining that Jalen Hurts' season was over because of diagnosis of blood clots, completed 21 of 31 passes for a career-best 331 yards.

national.title: Millions of wives in South Asia unprotected from marital rape - study
national.summary: More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia has not.
national.body:
Failure to fully criminalise marital rape leaves millions of women and girls unprotected in eight South Asian countries, where intimate partner violence is 35% higher than the global average, says a new study.

More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia - India, Afghanistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh - remain among the three dozen countries which haven't.

The only South Asian country where rape within marriage attracts the same penalty as any other rape is The Maldives.

Nepal and Bhutan have criminalised marital rape, but apply lesser penalties, says the study by Samaj, a coalition of women's rights groups in the region.

South Asia's marital rape laws largely stem from British colonial rule, says Ranjeeta Silwal of Equality Now, a global women's rights group part of Samaj.

The law, dating to 1860 in India and Bangladesh and 1885 in Sri Lanka, lists exceptions to rape - including sex by a man with his adult wife.

Campaigners say the law is outdated and forced sex is rape, regardless of the perpetrator. Experts warn marital sexual violence harms women's physical, psychological, emotional and sexual well-being.

More than 100 countries have criminalised marital rape, including the UK, which changed its law in 1991. But the exemption remains in India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.

national.title: Strobe Talbott, former Time magazine reporter and deputy secretary of state, has died
national.summary: Strobe Talbott, a former Time magazine reporter who later served as deputy secretary of state under President Bill Clinton and then headed the Brookings Institution, died Thursday. He was 80.
national.body:
FILE - Strobe Talbott, President Brookings Institution, speaks during a news conference in Berlin, July 16, 2008. Franka Bruns/AP hide caption

Strobe Talbott, a former Time magazine reporter who later served as deputy secretary of state under President Bill Clinton and then headed the Brookings Institution, died Thursday. He was 80.

His son, Devin Talbott, confirmed he passed away peacefully after a long illness in his East Hampton, New York, home.

The elder Talbott was educated at Yale and Oxford, where he bunked with Clinton. While at the British university, after interning for Time in Moscow, the magazine asked Talbott to help translate the leaked memoirs of Nikita Khrushchev, the former first secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union who was ousted in 1964.

FILE - President-elect Bill Clinton and Strobe Talbott of Time magazine talk privately as they walk along the beach on Hilton Head Island, S.C., Jan. 2, 1993. James Finley/AP hide caption

Talbott did, and it gave him some notoriety as a young man and a job at the magazine.

After 21 years at Time, where he focused on Soviet-American relations and held positions including Washington bureau chief and a foreign-affairs columnist, according to his U.S. State Department biography, he received a call from the newly elected Clinton.

Talbott joined the U.S. State Department in 1994, swiftly becoming deputy secretary of state. In that role, he was the architect of the Clinton administration's approach to Russia and other formerly Soviet countries and conducted negotiations between the U.S. and India after the latter's nuclear tests in 1998.

national.title: Inside Saudi Arabia, Houthi attacks test kingdom's image of security
national.summary: Despite the strikes, markets and restaurants in Riyadh remain busy as residents express trust in the government to protect them.
national.body:
Ten days after fleeing his home in Yemen's capital, Sanaa, Abu Khalil is selling socks on the streets of Riyadh.

"I walked out of Sanaa, I crossed the front line," he says, adding that he "hitched a ride into Saudi Arabia".

Families in Yemen are "struggling to provide for [their] children", he says, as he tries to earn enough to send some money home.

He asks us not to use his full name because his wife and four children are still in Sanaa, and he is frightened of what might happen to them if he is identified speaking out against the Houthis. "I ran away from the Houthis but I couldn't bring my family with me. May God protect them," he says.

Backed by Iran, the armed group has controlled much of northern Yemen since a civil war erupted more than a decade ago. It is fighting the internationally recognised government, which is supported by neighbouring Saudi Arabia.

And Saudi cities, such as Riyadh, are now coming under regular drone and missile attacks from the very group Abu Khalil fled.

An informal ceasefire in Yemen unravelled in July, and since the fighting escalated, the Houthis have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia. They have said they were retaliating against deadly Saudi air strikes in Yemen and what they say is a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled territory.

One Houthi strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured more than 300 - the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in years.

national.title: Major Thanksgiving storm brings flooding, flight delays across US
national.summary: Almost one million customers in the US had no power on Thursday evening as storms descended on both US coasts, bringing wind gusts, heavy rain and flooding.
national.body:
A massive Thanksgiving storm hammering the Midwest and north-east with heavy rain and winds, along with high tides out west, is causing widespread disruptions across the US.

More than 80 million Americans expected to be travelling this week. On Thursday 460 flights in the US were cancelled and another 2,508 flights into, out of, or within the US were delayed, tracking site FlightAware said.

The FAA has previously warned that delays would be possible "throughout the week" as a result of the rain and wind that are forecast.

Meanwhile, almost one million households were without power on Thursday night, with Pennsylvania, Maryland and Virginia the hardest hit states.

On Thursday, a powerful storm hit the eastern US, bringing damaging winds of up to 70mph, torrential rain, and major coastal flooding.

New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill declared a state of emergency as several communities along the Jersey Shore saw widespread flooding.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul also declared a state of emergency for New York City, Long Island and Westchester County.

In New York City, organisers of the annual Macy's Thanksgiving parade have postponed the event to Saturday.

national.title: New Zealand's ruling coalition falls short of parliamentary majority by one seat
national.summary: The right-leaning ruling bloc led by the National Party has fallen short of the majority needed to govern.
national.body:
New Zealand's ruling coalition has fallen short of a parliamentary majority by one seat, following a campaign shaped by a sluggish economy and disillusioned voters.

It now needs the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to remain in power. If they cannot reach a deal, the country may have to go back to the polls.

The incumbent National Party led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon secured 40 out of 130 seats, while its coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First took 13 and 12 respectively.

A government led by the centre-left Labour Party is not possible, official results on Friday show, as the bloc would not have enough seats even if Opportunity threw its weight behind it.

Luxon on Friday acknowledged that negotiations "may be challenging" and will take some time.

"Kiwis won't thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart or for sending them back to the polls," he told reporters.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said his party "ran an incredible campaign" but acknowledged that it doesn't have negotiating power despite winning the popular vote. "More New Zealanders voted for change at this election than for the status quo," he said.

New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions. Each person casts two votes – one for their preferred political party and another for their choice of local representative.

national.title: Trump to visit maker of semiconductor chips, including Nvidia's
national.summary: President Trump will visit the Phoenix TSMC facility, one of the largest manufacturers of advanced chips, including Nvidia's.
national.body: A White House official said Thursday that President Trump is planning to visit the groundbreaking of a Phoenix facility for a manufacturer of semiconductor chips, including for Nvidia, a trip that comes as the company is under increasing scrutiny for the president's involvement in reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO after he had an affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. On Dec. 4, Mr. Trump will tour and deliver remarks at the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company facility in Phoenix, Arizona, a White House official confirmed Thursday. The Taiwan-based company has been expanding in Arizona since 2020, according to the company's website, and next week's visit will be to the latest expansion of its facilities. A TSMC spokesperson also confirmed to CBS News in a statement that the president was expected to attend the groundbreaking. The White House official said the new expansion is expected to fund more than 10,000 direct jobs and another 11,000 indirect jobs in the surrounding community.It's unclear whether Arizona Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs or the state's Democratic Sens. Mark Kelly and Ruben Gallego would attend the event next week. The planned visit comes amid scrutiny of Nvidia, one of the world's most valuable companies, with its high-powered chips emerging as integral to the race for AI dominance between the U.S. and China. Co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang earlier this month resigned after the news broke of his alleged affair with Alice Huang, a former top executive at Singapore-based tech firm Megaspeed and who U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of spying for China. China has denied it.Mr. Trump advocated for Jensen Huang to be reinstated at Nvidia, with an official saying earlier this week that reinstating him would "preserve America's technological edge over China, strengthen our national security" and ensure the future of AI will be built in the U.S. Sources also told CBS News that Mr. Trump was privately concerned about the broader implications for the U.S. economy should Nvidia's value collapse. Nvidia's board reinstated Huang on Monday, and Mr. Trump touted his return in a social media post shortly afterward.

national.body: The Environmental Protection Agency said Thursday it expects to begin receiving sample results as early as Friday following the U.S. Army's detonation of a stockpile of degrading explosives at a munitions plant in Iowa. The EPA collected more than 1,500 air, water, soil and dust samples ahead of Wednesday's destruction of the lead azide stockpile, followed by more than 1,000 samples after the detonation, the agency said. Samples were sent to multiple EPA and private labs for testing. "The agency is expecting to start receiving lab results on post-detonation sampling as early as tomorrow," the EPA said in a news release.The EPA said it collected samples at more than 130 structures, including homes, schools, daycare centers and churches, as well as at parks, nearby farms, drinking water sources and the Mississippi River watershed.As of Thursday, no airborne lead had been detected throughout the region, the EPA said. The agency said it is also testing for other compounds that may have been released during the detonation."The agency is testing for everything we were anticipating could potentially be released as a result of the controlled detonation," it said in Thursday's news release. The Army on Wednesday detonated 5 tons of deteriorating explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant located in the small community of Middletown, citing the risk of an unplanned explosion. Local residents and environmental groups had sought to block the detonation over concerns that a plume of toxic lead dust could threaten public health and agriculture. The Middletown plant housed about 10,000 pounds of lead azide, which has been used in ammunition since World War I. The EPA said the lead azide had degraded over the last 20 years it had been in storage. It had undergone a recrystallization process that increased "the material's sensitivity to friction and shock" and made it more susceptible to the "risk of unintentional detonation," the EPA said. The 8th Circuit Court of Appeals temporarily halted the detonation last week while it considered whether to impose a longer-lasting ruling. national.body: One high school marching band from Texas says it has raised $350,000 to cover the cost of its 500-member group remaining in New York City after the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade was rescheduled until Saturday due to a potentially historic storm hitting the region on Thursday."It's been exhausting and emotional to figure this out, but it has been incredibly humbling to see an outpouring of kindness," Ryan Demkovich, the director of the Pride of Pearland Marching Band at Pearland High School in Texas, told CBS News about raising the funds required to cover the extended trip."I started scrambling through that," Demkovich said. "Can we find a hotel to stay in? Can we get our transportation back? How, at the last second on a holiday weekend, how astronomical are the prices going to be?" Other marching bands that traveled to New York from across the country are also raising money to cover the cost of their extended stays. For many of the high school musicians, the parade is a once-in-a-lifetime chance to perform for millions of spectators along the route and watching at home, and the postponement has made the trip significantly more expensive."This was quite a challenge for us, and there was a very frantic and large call to action to our community to let the kids stay here and finish it out," Demkovich added. In just the span of a few hours, the Pearland community came together to raise hundreds of thousands of dollars."They organized a fundraiser, they went on news stations, they broadcasted it, they posted it to get the word across," Pearland High School senior and band member Deborah James told CBS News. By Thursday, the band had raised enough money to pay for two extra nights at a hotel and to charter buses back to Texas after the parade on Saturday. national.title: Met Police ruined my life, says Kenyan man wrongly convicted over attack on UK couple
national.summary: Evidence from a British police officer helped convict Ali Kololo over a 2011 attack in the Kenyan resort of Lamu.
national.body:
A Kenyan woodcutter who was wrongly convicted and sentenced to death over an attack on a British couple has told the BBC that actions by London's Metropolitan Police involved in the case destroyed his life.

Somali gunmen broke into David and Judith Tebbutt's beach bungalow on the Kenyan coast in 2011. They shot David dead and abducted Judith, holding her captive in Somalia for six months.

Met detectives flew to Kenya to assist the investigation. Their evidence helped convict Ali Kololo, who spent more than a decade in prison before his conviction was overturned.

Kololo is suing the Met, claiming a senior officer, former Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, gave misleading evidence at his trial and acted unlawfully to secure his conviction.

In his first media interview, he told the BBC about his 15-year ordeal and his fight for compensation, which the Met is challenging in court.

We meet on Lamu, a small island off Kenya's northern coast, once a thriving Swahili port. People and goods are still carted through its narrow stone streets by donkey rather than car.

Standing at the jetty, where police once brought him ashore in handcuffs, he relishes being free. But he is struggling to rebuild his life.

"Everything was taken from me. I'm starting from zero. I don't think I'll ever go back to who I was before," he says.

national.title: Sheikh Hasina's planned return puts Bangladesh on edge - and India in a bind
national.summary: The ousted prime minister's December homecoming plan deepens Dhaka-Delhi tensions and risks fresh unrest.
national.body:
India correspondent Published 9 hours ago Sheikh Hasina has repeatedly vowed to return to Bangladesh.

Now the ousted prime minister has put a date on her homecoming - 16 December - and even outlined how she intends to make the journey.

The government in Dhaka, which had previously dismissed the prospect, is taking her latest declaration more seriously.

Hasina, 79, who fled to Delhi in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her 15-year rule, plans to go back on Victory Day, the anniversary of Bangladesh's triumph over Pakistan in the 1971 liberation war, her spokesperson said.

She was sentenced to death after being convicted of crimes against humanity for her role in the crackdown, in a trial held in her absence that raised questions about due process. Her Awami League party is banned in Bangladesh. The UN says as many as 1,400 people were killed by security forces during the uprising.

The government says she would be arrested immediately if she returned and has promised to carry out the death sentence.

Hasina now wants the Bangladesh government to arrange a flight from Delhi. If that fails, she could travel commercially or cross the land border.

"She is even prepared to walk into Bangladesh," Abu Obaidha Arin, a key aide to Hasina, told the BBC.

national.summary: A federal judge on Wednesday sided against Democrats on the federal government's taxpayer-funded ads that promoted partisan messages and President Donald Trump ahead of the midterm elections, declining to extend a temporary ban.
national.body:
Jesse Bedayn, Associated Press Jesse Bedayn, Associated Press

NEW YORK (AP) — A federal judge on Wednesday sided against Democrats on the federal government's taxpayer-funded ads that promoted partisan messages and President Donald Trump ahead of the midterm elections, declining to extend a temporary ban.

The Democratic National Committee had argued the TV spots were illegal government-sponsored propaganda intended to promote the president's campaign message just weeks before November's midterm elections. The ruling by U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan comes after another judge in a similar case in New York also declined a long-term ban on the ads.

AliKhan noted that a previous temporary restraining order against the ads had been issued when the election was less than a week away.

"But the November 2026 midterm elections have come and gone," she wrote, adding that the DNC was now claiming the party could be harmed by the ads in December congressional runoff elections or even because the 2028 presidential cycle has already begun.

AliKhan took issue with the DNC's argument that the "permanent" nature of campaigns justified an injunction against the ads.

"Such an argument, taken to its logical conclusion, would allow the DNC to seek preliminary relief in perpetuity because it could always point to the occurrence of some election somewhere in the country," she wrote.

Democrats sued the Trump administration in October after it began airing ads that were paid for at least in part by a $20 million Department of Homeland Security contract. In court papers, the DNC challenged at least 11 government-created ads that either aired on TV or appeared on Trump administration social media feeds.

national.summary: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited facilities that produce nuclear ingredients and called for building more nuclear weapons, days after ignoring U.S. President Donald Trump's offer to meet during his recent visit to Asia.
national.body:
Hyung-Jin Kim, Associated Press Hyung-Jin Kim, Associated Press

Kim Tong-Hyung, Associated Press Kim Tong-Hyung, Associated Press

SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited facilities that produce nuclear ingredients and called for building more nuclear weapons, days after ignoring U.S. President Donald Trump's offer to meet during his recent visit to Asia.

Experts say Kim likely wants to show off his evolving nuclear arsenal, the backbone of his authoritarian rule, and reaffirm his rejection of any future talks on dismantling his nuclear program.

The North's official Korean Central News Agency said Thursday that Kim inspected two nuclear materials production factories, one newly inaugurated and the other being expanded. KCNA photos showed Kim and senior military officials walking between dense rows of what appeared to be centrifuges used to produce weapons-grade uranium and touring halls displaying what were believed to be warheads. Some of the images were blurred.

KCNA said Kim visited a nuclear-powered equipment production base and a nuclear research institute as well on Wednesday.

North Korea has disclosed a uranium enrichment site a few times since it showed one at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex to visiting American scholars in 2010. North Korea didn't say where the nuclear materials production factories that Kim visited this week are located. In June, when North Korea disclosed parts of a uranium enrichment site while reporting on Kim's visit there, outside experts assessed it was likely an additional uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon.

Kim said his latest inspection visit was part of efforts to strengthen North Korea's defense capabilities in response to "variable nuclear threats approaching the Korean Peninsula moment by moment." He accused the U.S. of inciting its regional allies to possess nuclear-powered submarines and committing to sharing its nuclear weapons with them, KCNA said.

national.title: Mexico's most powerful cartels adapt as arrests and leadership battles reshape their ranks
national.summary: The arrest of another Mexican drug lord over the weekend added to a string of actions against cartels as Mexico intensifies its crackdown on organized crime under mounting pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump and with U.S. intelligence support.
national.body:
MEXICO CITY (AP) — The arrest of another Mexican drug lord over the weekend added to a string of actions against cartels as Mexico intensifies its crackdown on organized crime under mounting pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump and with U.S. intelligence support.

The capture of Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro," was hailed by both governments as a security win that may shift the balance of power within the Sinaloa Cartel. Yet violence persists among rival criminal groups across Mexico, where two powerful organizations — the Sinaloa Cartel and the Jalisco New Generation Cartel — continue to dominate the criminal landscape.

Both groups have been designated foreign terrorist organizations by the U.S., but experts say they still retain strong power in Mexico and abroad.

Here's a look at the balance of power between the two groups and how it has shifted under President Claudia Sheinbaum.

In late July 2024, two months before Sheinbaum took office, one of the Sinaloa Cartel's founders, Ismael "El Mayo" Zambada, was arrested in the U.S. following a Hollywood-esque airplane kidnapping orchestrated by "Los Chapitos," the sons of his former partner, Joaquín "El Chapo" Guzmán.

Shortly afterward, the Sinaloa Cartel plunged into a long-term internal war that continues to ravage the northern state of Sinaloa.

A year and a half later, the Mexican army killed Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, "El Mencho," leader of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel, or CJNG, one of Mexico's most powerful criminal groups. His death set off a violent response across 20 Mexican states that left more than 70 people dead, but it lasted only a few days.

The U.S. celebrated both operations. Zambada is serving a life sentence there, and two of his sons are cooperating with U.S. authorities. Mexico accused Washington of interference in the Zambada case although U.S. officials denied it.

Iran has denied responsibility for the attack, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying the incident looked "suspicious" and that Tehran would work with Kuwait and Italy to "determine the cause".

Kuwait's defence ministry said earlier that four people - the two Italians, a Kuwaiti national and Pakistani national - had been injured from falling shrapnel after a number of drones from Iran were detected and intercepted.

It comes just over a week after Kuwait said it had repelled overnight Iranian drone attacks on an airbase which hosts US forces - the first strikes in more than two months on the country.

Recent exchanges of fire between the US and Iran, and a deadlock in negotiations, have raised fears of a major escalation in the war.

The conflict began when US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, with Iran retaliating by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.

On Thursday, Araghchi said he had expressed condolences over the deaths in calls with his Italian and Kuwaiti counterparts and that the incident looked like a "precooked recipe for war", without expanding further.

national.title: What are king tides? These exceptionally high tides are increasingly flooding coastal communities
national.summary: King tides are the highest tides of the year, and they are increasingly flooding coastal communities as sea levels rise.
national.body:
Jennifer McDermott, Associated Press Jennifer McDermott, Associated Press

King tides are the highest tides of the year, and they are increasingly flooding coastal communities as sea levels rise.

King tide is a non-scientific or colloquial term that people often use to describe these exceptionally high tides. The 2026 super El Niño — the natural and temporary warming of parts of the Pacific — has raised coastal water levels and intensified the effects of king tides.

"Tides are incredibly complicated. Really every location has different tidal cycles and that's the basis for what a king tide is," said Alec Bogdanoff, an oceanographer and meteorologist in Fort Lauderdale, Florida. "It's a local term for the highest high tides of the year in a location. And when it impacts you, that's when they call it a king tide."

King tides typically occur when the sun, moon and Earth are nearly aligned because their gravitational pull adds together. This raises water levels and produces the greatest tidal effects of the year. This can happen on both coasts around the same time because the tides are responding to the same alignment and proximity of the moon and sun. In 2026, El Niño caused higher baseline water levels on both coasts, Bogdanoff said.

WATCH: King tides and strong waves destroy part of Pacifica pier as officials warn of coastal flooding

The highest high tides happen during full moons and new moons and seasonal cycles that can raise or lower sea levels, he added.

Historically, many coastal areas saw king tides once or twice a year, but some places are experiencing them more often than that as sea levels rise.

national.title: FCC says SpaceX can deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space. Scientists are skeptical
national.summary: The Trump administration on Wednesday gave SpaceX the green light to deploy 1 million satellites that it said would create data centers in space, a long-lofty goal of Elon Musk's rocket company, in a move that has raised both skepticism and alarm among some scientists.
national.body:
Wyatte Grantham-Philips, Associated Press Wyatte Grantham-Philips, Associated Press

The Trump administration on Wednesday gave SpaceX the green light to deploy 1 million satellites that it said would create data centers in space, a long-lofty goal of Elon Musk's rocket company, in a move that has raised both skepticism and alarm among some scientists.

The U.S. Federal Communications Commission lauded its authorization as a historic first amid the artificial intelligence race. It said that SpaceX's one million "orbital compute modules" (forming a data center constellation called "Starmind") would process massive amounts of data that would be used back on Earth — and bring humans closer to harnessing "the full power of the sun."

"America is leading the world into the era of super intelligence," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, who was appointed by Republican President Donald Trump, said in a statement. He added that Wednesday's move "opens a bold new frontier."

A lengthier authorization order published by the FCC noted that the company must deploy at least "one authorized space station" by 2033 — and then gradually add more and more through 2040. Musk welcomed the decision over social media.

The world's richest man has long vowed to form vast, solar-powered data centers in space to help run AI tools on Earth. But scientists and industry experts have stressed enormous technical and financial obstacles, as well as a host of environmental concerns.

Adam Becker, an astrophysicist and author, called the prospect of launching a million satellites into space to create data centers "a fantasy."

Proponents of data centers in space argue that capturing the sun's energy would ease pressure on power grids and cut demand for sprawling computing warehouses on Earth (and resources like water needed to cool them). Space seems to offer a solution because it is cold, but it is also a vacuum, trapping heat inside objects much like a thermos. Becker explained that there are "basic physical limits" to otherwise radiating that heat out — and sending lots of smaller satellites could potentially carry the necessary material combined, but it would be expensive and difficult.

national.title: 'Think twice': Banff officials issue warning over thin ice after skater's death
national.summary: After three separate incidents, one fatal, at Lake Louise, Parks Canada is warning visitors to be cautious after a warmer than average November.
national.body:
A 70-year-old resident of Banff, Alberta, has died after falling through ice on Lake Louise, prompting warnings about outdoor safety as Canada experiences warmer than normal November temperatures.

Police said the man, who has not been identified, was ice skating alone on Tuesday evening when he fell through thin ice. He was found two hours later by a rescue team and pronounced dead at a nearby hospital.

It comes after two other ice skaters fell in the lake's frigid waters on Monday, though both survived.

Canadian park authorities have issued a warning to visitors of the world-famous Banff National Park urging them to "think twice" before stepping on the ice.

"Visitors must be able to self-rescue should they fall in the water," Parks Canada said in a notice posted on Monday.

"If you choose to skate on natural ice, you do so at your own risk."

In a statement, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police offered condolences to the 70-year-old's family. It also warned the public of the dangers of being on the ice.

Parks Canada said that early season ice can be unpredictable, and that it does not actively monitor natural ice surfaces for safety or mark potential hazards.

national.title: Analysis: Why Trump's new tariffs are less of a threat
national.summary: Other countries have rerouted trade in response to his first tariff salvo, now they are looking beyond Trump's tenure.
national.body:
There was none of last April's fanfare, the Rose Garden reveal, the gameshow blue board or "Liberation Day" rhetoric surrounding Trump's tariff announcement this week.

Instead there is something rather tentative about this latest exercise with talk of further negotiations.

"We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC.

Around the world the view is that this week's announcement is an attempt to shore up the domestic legal underpinning of these tariffs, more than a fundamental change in the Trump trade agenda.

The tariffs are also not due to come in until January or possibly February, after a period of consultation. There has already been eight months of process and hearings, and the rates announced are upper ceilings, often up for negotiation. It's quite the contrast to the overnight shock meted out to the world last April.

Still, the US is making the argument that large swathes of the rest of the world, including allies, are harming the US goods trade position by supporting their own industries. This is the basis for the tariffs, in large part replacing the previous tariffs justified on "forced labour" provisions.

The UK, which was unaffected by the new tariff announcements, remains caught by the forced labour provisions, albeit at a rate of 10% extra on global tariffs. There was no move in response to the UK's digital services tax.

It means for many important countries there are now two legal bases upon which the Trump tariffs rest, after the Supreme Court struck down the original emergency basis earlier this year. A group of 25 states has taken the Trump administration to court to strike down the forced labour tariffs.

local.title: Holley woman embraces her heritage and newfound sense of identity
local.summary: Bailey Kleckner discovered another part of her ancestry when she and her mother moved in with her maternal grandmother, a member of the Onondaga Turtle Clan.
local.body:
If you had asked Bailey Kleckner five years ago who Two Clawing Turtles was, she wouldn’t have known — even though it was her all along.

“My given name is Two Clawing Turtles,” the 18-year-old said. “And that is to represent my two-spirit identity and also my fierceness as I have grown into my higher sense of being.”

Sitting at a picnic table at a park in Holley, Orleans County, Kleckner looks relaxed as she reflects on her journey.

“It was about five years ago now that I moved out here to Holley,” Kleckner said. “My story of even knowing my heritage really didn't start until I moved out here.”

Kleckner grew up in Chili, where she sensed there was something about her ancestry she didn't fully understand. It wasn't until her parents separated and she and her mother moved in with her maternal grandmother, a member of the Onondaga Turtle Clan, that she began to discover that part of herself.

“Not knowing for so long, that was really life-changing,” Kleckner said of learning more about her Indigenous heritage. “It made me feel like I was finally at home.”

She later would go through the process to become an official member of the tribe.

The Onondaga Nation, one of the original five nations of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, bases membership on maternal lineage, according to Brad Powless, an Onondaga Nation council member.

local.body:
Suzanne Schieres, lovingly known as Suzie, will be remembered for her strength, big heart, and unforgettable sense of humor. Famously funny, Suzie possessed a quick wit and sharp sense of humor that could instantly light up a room or put a smile on anyone's face.

Predeceased by parents, Edward and Geraldine Schieres and brothers, Nicholas, Michael, and Patrick. A beloved sister to Angela (Al) Valentin, Melissa (Edward) Mekus, Stephen (Karen) Schieres, a mother to Robert Glowniak and Kimberly (Jeffrey) Martin, grandmother to Taylesha, David and Julianna, great grandmother to Nalani and Bodi, and aunt of many. Suzie leaves behind a family and community who will forever cherish her love, laughter, and the memories they made together.

Suzie lived by a simple philosophy: "Have to have a good time in life because you can't take it with you." These words perfectly captured her spirit and the way she approached life. She believed in living every moment to the fullest, finding joy in the little things, laughing often, and making memories that would last a lifetime.

One of Suzie's greatest joys was Elvis Presley. She loved his music and especially adored singing along to her favorite song, "Love Me Tender." His music will forever remind her loved ones of her voice, her smile, and the joy she brought into their lives.

Though her passing leaves an immeasurable void, Suzie's legacy of love, resilience, and laughter will live on through the generations she leaves behind. Her family will carry her spirit forward in the stories they share, the memories they treasure, and the moments when they choose to embrace life just as she did.

Perhaps the best way to honor Suzie is to turn up the Elvis, sing along, laugh a little louder, love a little deeper, and remember her timeless advice to enjoy this beautiful, fleeting life.

Rest peacefully, forever in our hearts. May heaven be filled with Elvis music, and may you be singing along. You lived life to the fullest, and your love and laughter will never be forgotten.

Relatives and friends are welcome to attend Calling Hours on Saturday, November 28, 2026 from 2-6 p.m. at R. Mackowiak Funeral Home, Inc.; 56 East Doughty Street, Dunkirk, NY. Prayer services will begin at 5:30 p.m. Interment will be held privately in St. Joseph's Cemetery. Arrangements are by R. Michael Mackowiak III; R. Mackowiak Funeral Home, Inc. Audrey A. (Wilemski) McGill, 79, of Dunkirk, is at rest after a valiant fight with cancer on November 22, 2026. She was born in Dunkirk on December 29, 1946, she was the loving and caring wife of Danny McGill for 55 years.

An avid animal lover, she opened her heart and home to numerous stray cats over the years, giving them the love and care they deserved. She found enjoyment in watching beautiful sunsets and tending to her vegetable garden. Audrey was a member of the Dunkirk Senior Center and a parishioner of Blessed Mary Angela Church of St. Hyacinth.

Her family would like to extend a special thank you to her niece, Theresa Schrantz, Chautauqua Hospice & Palliative Care, and the staff at Chautauqua Nursing & Rehabilitation Center for the exceptional care, compassion, and kindness shown to Audrey. local.title: Steelers are turning to Rudolph to salvage season
local.summary: PITTSBURGH — A season on the brink of crumbling. A disgruntled quarterback unhappy with the state of things. A team in need of a jolt. Mason Rudolph has been here before, and a lot of other places, too, during a nearly decade-long career that’s consistently thrust him into uncomfortable situations.
local.body:
PITTSBURGH -- A season on the brink of crumbling. A disgruntled quarterback unhappy with the state of things. A team in need of a jolt.

Mason Rudolph has been here before, and a lot of other places, too, during a nearly decade-long career that’s consistently thrust him into uncomfortable situations.

When Rudolph trots onto the field on Friday for the chaos-laden Pittsburgh Steelers (6-4) as they host Denver (8-2), he’ll be replacing a good friend and mentor in Aaron Rodgers, whose ugly departure this week shook one of the NFL’s proudest franchises to its very foundation.

And he’ll do it while playing for a head coach in Mike McCarthy whose reputation was forever tarnished and locker room presence diminished -- at least temporarily -- following Rodgers’ scorched-earth appearance on “The Pat McAfee Show” following the four-time MVP’s stunning benching and dismissal.

“Does it put some of us in an awkward space? Yes,” Rudolph said at the end of a dizzying 24 hours when he was thrust from trusted backup to starter. “But, again, it’s just another sort of opportunity to overcome adversity, and I think we’ll all look back on this as good experience.”

Or at least a defining one for both Rudolph and the current iteration of the Steelers.

If there’s anyone uniquely qualified for the challenge of picking up the pieces, it’s Rudolph. The checklist of things Rudolph has endured since being selected in the third round of the 2018 draft reads like something straight of Shakespeare.

There was the ugly brawl in Cleveland in 2019 that ended with then-Browns defensive tackle Myles Garrett ripping off Rudolph’s helmet and swinging it at him. There was his subsequent benching for undrafted rookie free agent Duck Hodges. There was the tie against Detroit in 2021 when he made a spot start after Ben Roethlisberger tested positive for COVID-19 less than 24 hours before kickoff. There was the promise that he was in the mix to be Roethlisberger’s successor in the spring of 2022, only to have the team sign Mitch Trubisky, then draft Kenny Pickett and bump Rudolph to the third string.

local.title: Sherman sets date for village dissolution vote
local.summary: Village of Sherman Board of Trustees, at their meeting this month, approved a resolution setting a date for a referendum on the possible dissolution of the village. local.body:
Village of Sherman Board of Trustees, at their meeting this month, approved a resolution setting a date for a referendum on the possible dissolution of the village.

The referendum, which uses the New York state mandated phrasing, reads: Shall the Village of Sherman, NY be dissolved? Village residents will vote yes or no to the question on Tuesday, Feb. 9 from 6 a.m. until 9 p.m. in the fire hall.

Prior to approving the resolution for the referendum, village trustees approved a resolution accepting and recording the valid citizen-initiated petition calling for the dissolution of the village. Village Clerk/Treasurer Jeanette Ramm confirmed that 145 out of 151 signatures on the petition were residents of the village and the village attorney found no deficiencies with the petition.

A certified letter confirming the validation was sent to Sue Oehlbeck who organized the citizen initiative petition, confirming the validation. “The process begins after our resolution tonight,” said Village Mayor Colleen Meeder.

The village will apply for a Citizens’ Re-Organization Empowerment Grant, administered by the state Department of State, which can provide up to 90% reimbursement funding for the process, up to a maximum of $25,000.

Trustees also authorized the village to retain a specialized municipal planning consultant to draft an objective pre-referendum study. This study includes an inventory of village assets, liabilities, structural service models and public informational reporting.

Meeder said that she and Ramm have already contacted the post office concerning a bulk mailing to all residents. However, a one-time bulk mailing would be more expensive than first class postage. Also, Meeder said, some residents have PO boxes, which are not accessible by the village. “There is no good way to do this. We’re trying to get out as much information as we can,” she said.

In a related matter, Meeder said the village is combatting the misinformation and the false narratives regarding the Sherman solar array. Rumors abound that the village is nearly bankrupt and that both companies involved in the solar array have filed for bankruptcy, she said.

local.body:
HANOVER -- The city of Dunkirk is not the only municipality set to lose its Community Bank branch in the coming months. The Town of Hanover was recently notified that the Silver Creek branch, located at Main Street and Central Avenue, is set to close in early 2027.

"Unfortunately, Community Bank is closing. We've received a letter," Lou Pelletter, Hanover Town Supervisor, said at a recent meeting. "We're going to be taking a look at what our future looks like with that."

Community Bank recently announced plans to close its Central Avenue branch in Dunkirk, consolidating its banking services at the Vineyard Drive location in the Town of Dunkirk effective Friday, March 19. Silver Creek and Hanover customers are now in the same boat as Dunkirk's customers. Community Bank said the decision was made following a thorough assessment of its branch network and how it can best serve customers as banking needs evolve.

Within eyesight of Community Bank is another recently closed business in the heart of Silver Creek, the former Rite Aid pharmacy. Pelletter recently met with Silver Creek Mayor Kathy Tampio, Deputy Mayor Jeff Hornburg, and a representative from the County of Chautauqua Industrial Development Agency (CCIDA) to discuss avenues for a new pharmacy to be located within the Town of Hanover.

At the recent meeting with the Village and the CCIDA, Pelletter provided all of the information he gathered from his efforts since Rite Aid closed. Pelletter previously spoke with Michael Pease, CEO of The Chautauqua Center, about expanding the center's Waterfront Pharmacy into the area. Pelletter remains optimistic about what could come next.

At its latest meeting, the Town Board approved new healthcare plans for eligible active employees and retirees. Active employees have a choice between Univera Bronze and Univera Gold plans, beginning Dec. 1. Retirees have the choice between Univera Senior Choice and Highmark of WNY Medicare Forever Blue, beginning Jan. 1, 2027. The Town covers 100% of the deductible costs for the Univera Bronze plan for active employees. The plans are in place of Independent Health, the Town's previous provider.

The Town Board also regretfully accepted the resignation of James Pinkowski as Hanover Court Attendant, effective Dec. 31.

In the month of October, the Town Clerk's Office collected $1,204 in State, County, and local revenue. The Clerk's Office issued 159 State Department of Environmental Conservation licenses, tags and permits; 41 dog licenses; three marriage licenses; and 11 handicap tags. The Code Enforcement Office issued 19 permits, of which 15 were in the Town and four were in the Village of Silver Creek, amounting to $1,200 in revenue for the Town.

local.body:
Early voting had already been underway for five days in late October when county and state Republicans gathered for a rally in Lakewood for what was to be a final push for the Nov. 3 election. One of the slogans used at the event matched those on signs scattered across lawns in Chautauqua County: "Fire Hochul."

Though this corner understands the sentiment and frustration, politics is unquestionably filled with retribution. In our staunchly red district, there are a cornucopia of reasons to be disappointed with how Gov. Kathy Hochul oversees the Empire State.

Her policies are often too far left for residents here who hold traditional beliefs. She is also pictured far too often with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, public enemy No. 1 when it comes to concerns about the nation moving toward socialism.

On the flip side, as a native Western New Yorker, she remains generous in supporting a number of economic causes in the region. Within the last year, the governor supported construction of a new north county hospital and played a role in expansion plans for Wells Enterprises in Dunkirk. Additionally, in June, she congratulated Jamestown for winning $10 million in Downtown Revitalization Initiative funding and Falconer for receiving another $4.5 million through NY Forward.

Despite these criticisms, one characteristic Hochul does not have is being delusional. Leave that to the chairman of the state Republican Party.

Within hours of overseeing another statewide shutout, Ed Cox demonstrated his obliviousness in a simple statement. "While Republicans fielded one of the best statewide tickets in living memory, we were not able to overcome the national political environment," he said. "Midterm elections are historically difficult for the party holding the presidency, especially in a second term."

Cox is a master at making excuses. His leadership -- as this corner has noted in the past -- is about as realistic as February camping in Western New York.

Republicans were not only thumped in traditionally blue New York, but they also were unseated across America in bastions that had been consistently loyal to the Grand Old Party. High gas and food prices, tied to an unpopular war with Iran, turned the tables nationally.

local.title: After big wins, pressure ramps up on Dems
local.summary: The final tallies are coming in, and the result is extraordinary. As of Sunday, Democrats have won the largest House majority in a national election for either party in three decades. Their Senate majority is the largest since 1992. They’ve even seized control of a majority of statehouses across the
local.body:
The final tallies are coming in, and the result is extraordinary. As of Sunday, Democrats have won the largest House majority in a national election for either party in three decades. Their Senate majority is the largest since 1992. They’ve even seized control of a majority of statehouses across the country.

All the more remarkable because they had to overcome gerrymandering by Republican-led state legislatures, ICE arrests, and Trump threats.

Hakeem Jeffries, who will be Speaker of the House, said on Sunday: “The people of our great country delivered House Democrats a historic majority with a mandate to fight for an Affordable America. Together, we will work hard to deliver the dramatic change in direction the American people are demanding.”

I don’t want to rain on Jeffries’ parade, but I don’t think this is what Democrats ought to be saying now.

Voters who have elected Democrats may think Democrats will be able to deliver “dramatic change,” but I don’t see how Dems can deliver dramatic change with Trump still in the White House holding a veto pen — and surrounded by belligerent fanatics like Stephen Miller, JD Vance, Pete Hegseth, RFK Jr., and Todd Blanche. And when, behind them, the American oligarchy still has the reins of power.

Democrats have won by big margins, but not big enough to override Trump’s vetoes or the oligarchs’ preferences.

I’m concerned about the presidential election of 2028 when — after not getting anything done for two years and being blamed by Trump, Miller, Vance, et al. for everything that goes wrong in America — Democrats have to convince voters that they’re still the party of change that voters opted for in the 2026 midterms.

I speak from experience. The last time one party prevailed to this degree in a national election was in 1992. I was there, and I accompanied Clinton to Washington. The economy was shite. Expectations were sky-high for a sudden recovery, along with fundamental reform of healthcare, education, and much else.

local.title: Local health official recommends vaccinating infants against measles sooner
local.summary: The Monroe County health department wants children to get the measles, mumps and rubella vaccines as soon as 6 months old.
local.body:
The Monroe County health department is recommending that pediatricians start giving the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine to infants as early as 6 months old.

The MMR vaccine requires two doses. The first shot is routinely given at 12 months and the second one between four and six years old.

Dr. Marielena Vélez de Brown, Monroe County public health commissioner, issued the recommendation to vaccinate children earlier in response to the uptick in measles cases locally and abroad.

"We do have an increased risk of being exposed for our residents here, and that's why I have made this decision to make this recommendation for our local population," Vélez de Brown said during a news conference Tuesday.

She added that although no cases have originated in Monroe County, patients from nearby counties often seek medical attention in the area risking transmission within the community.

Vélez de Brown issued the recommendations right before the holiday season.

"Getting the early vaccine will help them (infants) develop their protection even earlier as we all gather in different parts of the country where there are numerous outbreaks occurring," Vélez de Brown said.

Patients who receive the early vaccine, she added, still need to take their routine shot at 12 months. For those who get their first dose at 12 months, officials recommend getting the second dose at least 28 days later instead of waiting four years.

local.body: More than 14,000 runners took on Buffalo's 131st Annual YMCA Turkey Trot Thursday, and this year they faced a brand new route. The race is a highlight of Buffalo's running calendar and a Thanksgiving tradition dating back to 1896. But this year runners lined up behind a new downtown start line as the 5-mile race took a new circular route. Previously a point-to-point route, the new course was created this year after the former start point, the Delaware Avenue branch of the YMCA, closed down.Runners and walkers of all ages and abilities took to the course Thursday, including a few canine companions. Christopher Bertola of Orchard Park was the first to cross the finish line, with a time of 24:14. He gave the new route a thumbs up. "I like it honestly, it's a fast course, it's flat," Bertola said. local.summary: The family behind the Blizzard of '77 Travel Game is bringing back this unique piece of Buffalo history to commemorate the upcoming 50th anniversary of those five fateful winter days.
local.body: The family behind the Blizzard of '77 Travel Game is bringing back this unique piece of Buffalo history to commemorate the upcoming 50th anniversary of those five fateful winter days.On the morning of January 28, 1977, just after 11 a.m., the blizzard began. Over the next few days, Buffalo and surrounding areas saw snow fall as high as 100 inches, with high winds creating drifts as high as 30 to 40 feet. The weather was so severe that President Jimmy Carter declared an "emergency" for the entire states of New York and Pennsylvania, the first time a snowstorm had prompted such a response.At the time, Buffalo resident Paul Marino was only nine years old."My dad, he was a salesman, and we were living in Buffalo, and he drove down to Jamestown the morning of the blizzard," Paul told WKBW. "He was coming back from his morning appointment. Around 11:10 a.m. is when the storm actually struck."According to Paul, his father, Chuck Marino, found the thruway route impassable. Attempting to turn around, Chuck found a handful of other motorists who had been stranded due to the worsening conditions. Eventually, he and the other travelers took refuge from the storm at a fire station in Irving for two days."During that time, we (Paul and his mother Donna) would check in with him; he'd give us a call, and he was explaining to us, Mom and I, what that experience was like trying to drive that." Paul continued, "My parents always loved playing games with me; they always encouraged creativity, so I took one of my dad's legal pads, and he hated when I did this, but I ripped off all of the paper so I could have the cardboard, right? I've got the cardboard, I grabbed some of my markers and my Matchbox cars."Paul would go on to draw a road, including snow drifts, abandoned cars, dead batteries, and other obstacles his father had witnessed firsthand. When Chuck returned home and saw his son's creation, that moment inspired the Blizzard of '77 Travel Game.The original Blizzard of '77 Travel Game moved remarkably quickly from idea to market. Released in July 1977, the first production run of 40,000 games sold out almost immediately. A second run followed, bringing total sales of the original Buffalo edition to more than 70,000 games.Following these initial releases, no further copies of the game would be made. local.title: Genesee partners with Foodlink for Keg Tree food drive
local.summary: The first 200 people who attend the annual Keg Tree lighting with three nonperishable food items will receive a free commemorative mug.
local.body:
The Genesee Brewery is partnering with Foodlink for the first time to turn its annual Keg Tree lighting into a food drive.

The first 200 people who arrive to the event on Dec. 4 with three non-perishable food items will receive a free mug, shaped like a keg and etched with a picture of the Keg Tree. The food drive will continue through the holiday season at the Genesee Brew House.

Mark Dwyer at Foodlink said the event comes at a pivotal time for food insecurity in Rochester.

"It's a great chance to just raise awareness locally for not only Foodlink and the work that we do, but just the issue of food insecurity that impacts thousands of our neighbors," Dwyer said.

Foodlink tracks data from all of the food pantries in its network around the region. Dwyer said that the numbers of people visiting food pantries from August and September were the highest the nonprofit has ever seen. Those months also saw a 13% increase in food pantry usage compared to the previous year.

"What's on everyone's mind: food, fuel, prices are sky high," Dwyer said. "Just inflation and the economy are continuing to impact people's ability to put food on the table."

The Genesee Brewery approached Foodlink to partner at Keg Tree. Carl Falk, general manager for the Genesee Brew House, said the plan is to focus the company on giving back to the Rochester community.

"Foodlink has been such a staple in our community, helping people, and obviously this time of year there's an even greater emphasis on being a community partner," Falk said.

entertainment.title: ‘Charlie Brown’ voice actor received zero residuals for nearly 50 years due to banned ’70s contract
entertainment.summary: It turns out the voice of Charlie Brown didn't even make peanuts in residuals.
entertainment.body:
Good grief — it turns out the voice of Charlie Brown didn’t even make peanuts in residuals.

Todd Barbee was just 10 when his father’s connection to producer Lee Mendelson landed him the iconic role of Charlie Brown in 1973’s “A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving.”

Generations grew up watching his performance on network TV, yet Barbee, now 63, revealed to host Joseph Sibilia on his podcast, “Nostalgia Tonight with Joe Sibilia,” that he didn’t receive residual checks until about six years ago.

“Aside from the bountiful residuals I’m sure you’ve collected for the last 50-plus years, what has been the most rewarding part of being a part of the ‘Peanuts’ legacy?” Sibilia asked Barbee.

“Well, let me correct you on one front,” Barbee replied. “We were actually under an old contractual relationship from the ’70s that is no longer allowed by Screen Actors Guild and AFTRA, which is American Federation of Television and Radio Artists. The contract was a buyout, and that is not allowed by the unions anymore. I think it was overturned in the ’80s.”

“So, we did not receive any residuals at all,” Barbee noted. “In fact, I didn’t receive a single residual until about six years ago.”

The initial gig paid “pretty handsomely” at the time “in 1970 dollars.” He used his paycheck to help his mother buy the house that she still lives in to this day after his parents divorced. However, he didn’t see any residual checks, no matter how massive the special became as a holiday tradition.

“Peanuts” made its debut on Oct. 2, 1950. The travails of the “little round-headed kid” Charlie Brown and his pals eventually ran in more than 2,600 newspapers, reaching millions of readers in 75 countries.

entertainment.title: John Farnham’s Family Gives Rare Update on Legendary Singer’s Health
entertainment.summary: Farnham continues to stay out of the spotlight after undergoing marathon surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his throat in 2022.
entertainment.body:
John Farnham ’s spirits remain high, his mind is sharp, but his body is failing. That’s the gist of a rare health update, shared from the legendary Australian singer’s family. Explore John Farnham See latest videos, charts and news

These days, the veteran singer is at home but gets around in a wheelchair and requires oxygen.

“His mental state is really good,” Rob Farnham, John’s son, told 102.5 ABC Perth Breakfast . “He’s spending a lot of time with his grandson whom he loves. He’s doing a lot of physical therapy. He’s happy, he’s laughing, he’s joking.” Related Miranda Lambert Heats Up Halftime at Dallas Cowboys' NFL Thanksgiving Game: Watch Anuel AA's 'RHLM2' Album Is Finally Here: 'I Made It With My Heart and Soul' Lana Del Rey Says New Albums Are 'Getting Close' to Completion: 'I'm Happy With Them'

John Farnham’s wife is a constant at his side. “Mum definitely sacrifices herself for dad and to help dad and she’s an amazing woman and we’re very proud of her as well,” Rob Farnham explains. “Obviously sometimes she gets a bit down but she has us to lean on and that’s what your family support is.”

The revered pop singer continues to stay out of the spotlight after undergoing marathon surgery in 2022 to remove a cancerous tumor from his throat. He will never sing again, his reps confirmed in May, but the time away from the public glare hasn’t dimmed his superstar status in these parts.

Farnham was the focus of an all-star concert at Melbourne’s Rod Laver Arena on Sept. 20, featuring 120 artists and musicians, all of them selected by Farnham. The concert, a swift sellout, was cinecast into Hoyt’s theaters and served as a fundraiser for Head and Neck Cancer Australia . He was unable to attend, due to his condition. And when a jukebox musical based on Farnham’s career premiered recently in Sydney , he stayed away, which prompted the health update.

With 1986’s Whispering Jack, Farnham orchestrated one of the all-time great comebacks. The album spent 25 weeks at No. 1 in Australia, en route to shifting more than one million copies, becoming the first domestic LP to do so. It remains the highest-selling album ever in Australia by a local talent.

Whispering Jack, of course, features Farnham’s signature song, “You’re The Voice,” a top 10 hit in the United Kingdom, and, four decades on, the unofficial anthem of Australia. He was named Australian of the Year in 1987, was named Officer of the Order of Australia in 1996, was inducted into the ARIA Hall of Fame in 2003 and has collected 19 career ARIA Awards.

You can’t choose you family. But you can choose your true family . That’s how Nile Rodgers remembers Andy Taylor , the founding guitarist of Duran Duran and The Power Station, who died this week following a years-long battle with prostate cancer, at the age of 65 . “Dear Andy Taylor RIP. How many countless great days and nights did we have?,” he writes. “I was sleeping last night when I heard the news of your passing. #RIP my dear friend. We were always happy when we were together. I love you.”

Rodgers and Taylor go way back. The Chic mainstay and elite record producer worked with Duran Duran on many of their hits, a friendship that began with the British new wave legends’ first U.S. No. 1 “The Reflex” from 1984.

Chic’s bass player Bernard Edwards produced the 1985 debut album from The Power Station, which gathered Duran Duran’s Andy and John Taylor, along with English singer Robert Palmer and U.S. drummer Tony Thompson. Rodgers provided some informal assistance to the project, which yielded the hits “Some Like It Hot” and a cover of Marc Bolan’s “Get It On (Bang A Gong)”.

“ #BernardEdwardsRIP loved you, and #TonyThompsonRIP loved you,” adds Rodgers, a cancer survivor. “Our two bands will be forever linked in the most special way. True family. Peace and eternal love.”

Rodgers shared a happy snap of himself with Andy, from somewhere, sometime in the 1980s, slapped with the caption: “The way I’ll always think of us…guitarist brothers.”

entertainment.title: 2027 BRIT Awards Trophy Designed by ‘One of Britain’s Greatest Living Artists’: See Photos
entertainment.summary: The trophy will be presented to winners at the ceremony on Feb. 27 in Manchester.
entertainment.body:
The 2027 BRIT Awards trophy has been designed by former Turner Prize-winning visual artist Dame Rachel Whiteread (Nov. 27).

Each year a different designer shapes a distinct creative vision for their trophy, modeled on the image of Britannia, traditionally represented by a female warrior with a shield and helmet.

In recent years, the trophy has been designed by iconic names such as Dame Vivienne Westwood, Sir Peter Blake, Tracey Emin, Dame Zaha Hadid, and last year’s designer, Matthew Williamson. Related Miranda Lambert Heats Up Halftime at Dallas Cowboys' NFL Thanksgiving Game: Watch Anuel AA's 'RHLM2' Album Is Finally Here: 'I Made It With My Heart and Soul' Lana Del Rey Says New Albums Are 'Getting Close' to Completion: 'I'm Happy With Them' Explore Billboard See latest videos, charts and news

Whiteread took on 2027’s assignment, and her trophy will be presented to winners at the ceremony on Feb. 27 at the Co-op Live in Manchester.

In 1993, Whiteread became the first woman to win the Turner Prize, an accolade presented annually to a British visual artist; previous victors include Damien Hirst, Gilbert & George, and Anish Kapoor. Four years after her win, in 1997, she was the first woman to represent Britain at the Venice Biennale.

Her work primarily focuses on casting, and her Turner Prize-winning exhibit House (1993) featured a life-sized concrete cast of a Victorian terraced house in east London. Whiteread’s work has been exhibited in the Tate Museum, Paris’ Centre Pompidou and New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Museum of Modern Art.

Whiteread’s vision for the 2027 trophy features a steely, silver frame with holes punctuated throughout a silver frame alongside holes. “I used the motif of the BRIT Award and tried to change it in some way,” she said in a statement. “I exposed the interior of the statue – as an artist would do with their music.”

Speaking on the appointment, Glyn Aikins , co-president of RCA Records at Sony Music U.K., called Whiteread one of “Britain’s greatest living artists.” He added, “Rachel has created something that is unmistakably her own and is a fitting tribute to the limitless imagination of the artists we celebrate each year and that also captures what the BRITs stands for in celebrating the very best of British creativity. The artists who lift this trophy will be holding a genuine work of art.”

In a moment, we'll want to know what you thought about Episode 8. But first, a quick recap.

Episode 7 ended with Rapp (Noah Reid), whom the Parks fired, learning that Katherine (Carrie-Anne Moss) is the daughter of Olena (Sheila McCarthy). He then theorized that Pam (Ezra Franky) was therefore Katherine's daughter, and that all three of them were planning to kill Eckert (Patrick Gilmore) — aka the third "bad dog" Olena referenced after Henry ( Hudson Williams ) and Logan (Hudson Williams) — in the woods. So he drove out to try to find the cabin, leaving a voicemail explaining everything to Carson (Clark Backo) on the way.

The finale begins with Rapp out in the trees, shining his flashlight around and seeing nothing — though he has flashes of visions of three women wearing masks like he found in Pam's room. "Turn your back to the forest and your face to me," he recites from his notes, then tries it in Ukranian three times as the women in masks approach. There's a rush of wings and then a bunch of chickens appear, seemingly lining the path to the foul-footed hut he's been trying to summon. He drops his lighter on the ground — ostensibly for Carson to find as a breadcrumb? — and takes off down the path.

Courtesy of AMC+ The chickens lead Rapp to a shack filled with candles and hanging bones. As he peers into the window, he sees Katherine tending to her mother. But then, all of a sudden, they're both behind him, commandeering his gun and marching him inside. "You're just in time for the big show," Katherine says, tying him to a chair while Olena — who seems to be drifting in and out of lucidity — holds the gun on him.

Rapp says he knows that Pam, who is Anna, is planning to have a baby with Eckert and then kill him. "You've got it all figured out," Katherine says in a tone that suggests otherwise.

As Carson and Eckert enter the forest, she asks him again if he had anything to do with covering up LIly's assault and hurting Geena (Megan Follows). "I mean, we had words," he says feebly, and Carson realizes that her boss did, indeed, do all the things of which he's accused. He counters that he didn't mean to break Geena's wrist. Sorry, dude, no partial credit on this test.
